prompt: Which word or phrase correctly completes the sentence?
passage: By the time the guests arrive tonight, Grandpa ____ the whole turkey.
why_wrong: uses the present perfect, ignoring that the reference point (tonight) is in the future
uses the past perfect, which needs a past reference point
uses the simple present and loses the sense of an action completed before another
explanation: "By the time the guests arrive tonight" sets a future reference point, and the carving will be complete before it, so the future perfect "will have carved" is needed. "Has carved" and "had carved" point to the present and the past, and "carves" does not show completion before the arrival.

prompt: Which word correctly completes the sentence?
passage: Not only did Lily water the tomatoes, ____ she also pulled every weed along the fence.
why_wrong: treats "not only" as plain addition and reaches for "and"
picks a coordinator without matching it to the correlative pair
chooses "yet" because it feels close to "but", though only "but" completes "not only ... but also"
explanation: "Not only" pairs with "but (also)" as a correlative conjunction. "And", "or" and "yet" do not complete the pair.

prompt: Which word or phrase correctly completes the sentence?
passage: Ana kept practicing the song ____ her fingers were sore, because the recital was only two days away.
why_wrong: repeats the cause relation that the end of the sentence already gives, though sore fingers are not a reason to keep practicing
reads the sore fingers as a goal of the practice
sets up a condition that makes the practicing depend on her fingers, which the sentence does not say
explanation: Sore fingers would normally make someone stop, so the clause concedes a difficulty: "even though". The reason she practiced is given later ("because the recital was ... away"), so "because" does not fit here, "so that" makes soreness her goal, and "unless" makes no sense.

prompt: Which word or phrase correctly completes the sentence?
passage: If it ____ tomorrow, the bike trip to the lake will be moved to Sunday.
why_wrong: puts "will" in the if-clause because the event is in the future
uses the past tense, which belongs to an imagined condition with "would" in the main clause
uses the conditional "would", which does not match "will be moved"
explanation: In a real future condition the if-clause takes the simple present and the main clause takes "will": "If it rains tomorrow, the trip will be moved." "Will rain" and "would rain" do not belong in this if-clause, and "rained" signals an unreal condition.

prompt: Which word or phrase correctly completes the sentence?
passage: Every Saturday, Mia's family drives to the farmers' market, where Mia ____ the freshest peaches she can find.
why_wrong: shifts into the past although "drives" and "can find" describe a present habit
uses the present perfect, which reports a finished action rather than a weekly habit
uses the past perfect, which needs an earlier past event
explanation: "Every Saturday", "drives" and "can find" describe a present habit, so the verb stays in the simple present: "picks". The other forms shift the time of the action.

prompt: Which choice correctly replaces the bracketed words?
passage: Before the storm reached our street last night, Dad [has already brought] the patio chairs inside.
why_wrong: keeps the present perfect, which cannot sit with "last night"
shifts to the present tense in a sentence about last night
uses the future for an action that happened last night
explanation: The chairs were brought in before another past event (the storm reaching the street), so the past perfect "had already brought" is correct. The present perfect, present and future do not fit "last night".

prompt: Which choice correctly replaces the bracketed words?
passage: For the science fair, Theo will build [either a model volcano nor] a small weather station.
why_wrong: switches to "neither" but keeps the mismatched partner, and also changes the meaning to building nothing
keeps the mismatched pair "either ... nor"
pairs "both" with "or" instead of "and"
explanation: "Either" pairs with "or". "Either ... nor", "neither ... or" and "both ... or" are mismatched pairs.

prompt: Which choice correctly replaces the bracketed words?
passage: When the bell rang, the students [had finished] their spelling quiz and were waiting quietly for the next lesson.
why_wrong: uses the present perfect in a sentence set in the past ("rang", "were waiting")
uses the future perfect for an event already over
uses the present tense, which clashes with "rang"
explanation: The quiz was done before the bell rang, another past event, so the original past perfect "had finished" is already correct. The other forms move the action into the present or future.

prompt: Which choice correctly replaces the bracketed word?
passage: Leo opened the oven, checked the bread, and [sees] that the crust was perfectly golden.
why_wrong: keeps a shift into the present inside a series of past actions
uses the present perfect, which breaks the past-tense series
jumps to the future in the middle of a finished sequence
explanation: "Opened", "checked" and "was" are past tense, so the third verb in the series must be too: "saw". The other choices shift tense without a reason.

prompt: Which choice correctly replaces the bracketed word?
passage: The garden hose was too short to reach the back fence, [but] Grandma bought a longer one at the hardware store.
why_wrong: keeps a contrast word, though buying a longer hose follows from the short one
offers a choice between two events that both happened
uses "nor", which joins two negative ideas
explanation: Grandma bought a longer hose because the old one was too short, so the second clause is a result: "so". "But" signals contrast, "or" an alternative, and "nor" a second negative.

prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
choices: By next June, my cousin will have lived in Denver for three years.
Omar had already eaten lunch when his friends invited him for pizza.
Since last spring, Hana has taken swimming lessons every Tuesday.
Yesterday, Priya has finished her mystery novel.
why_wrong: mistakes the correct future perfect for an error because it has three verb words
thinks the past perfect is wrong because both events are in the past
thinks the present perfect cannot be used with "since"
explanation: The present perfect ("has finished") cannot be used with a finished past time like "yesterday"; it should be "finished". The future perfect with "by next June", the past perfect before another past event, and the present perfect with "since last spring" are all correct.

prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
choices: Neither the coach nor the players expected the game to go into overtime.
Whether we take the bus or ride our bikes, we will reach the park by noon.
Ben wanted either to visit the aquarium nor to see the new movie.
Both the library and the museum close early on holidays.
why_wrong: thinks "neither ... nor" is a double negative
does not recognize "whether ... or" as a correlative pair
thinks "both ... and" needs a singular verb
explanation: "Either" must pair with "or", so "either to visit ... nor to see" is an error. "Neither ... nor", "whether ... or" and "both ... and" are used correctly.

prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
choices: Wow, that kite is flying higher than the school roof.
Sam forgot his umbrella, although he got soaked.
Although the trail was muddy, the hikers reached the waterfall.
Lily stayed inside because the wind was cold and strong.
why_wrong: thinks an interjection cannot begin a sentence
thinks a sentence cannot begin with "although"
thinks "because" cannot join two clauses
explanation: Getting soaked is the result of forgetting the umbrella, so "although" (which signals contrast) is the wrong conjunction; "so" fits. The interjection "Wow", the opening "Although" clause and "because" are all used correctly.

prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
choices: Nora mixed the batter while her brother greased the pan.
The movie starts at seven, so we are leaving at six-thirty.
Every morning the rooster crows before anyone in the house wakes up.
Jack climbs to the top of the rope, rings the bell, and slid back down.
why_wrong: thinks two past actions joined by "while" need different tenses
thinks the present tense cannot describe a scheduled event
thinks "crows" and "wakes" should be in the past
explanation: "Climbs" and "rings" are present tense, so "slid" shifts tense for no reason; it should be "slides". The other sentences keep their tenses consistent.

prompt: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: By the time the movie ended, the popcorn has run out.
Max has visited his grandmother last weekend.
Ivy will have finished her chores before her friends arrive.
When we got to the station, the train already leaves.
why_wrong: uses the present perfect where the past perfect is needed before "ended"
uses the present perfect with the finished time "last weekend"
uses the present tense for an action finished before another past event
explanation: "Will have finished ... before her friends arrive" correctly uses the future perfect. The others need "had run out", "visited" and "had already left".

prompt: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: Zoe can neither swim or dive, but she loves the beach.
Whether the sun shines or not, the parade will go on.
The recipe calls for either butter and oil, not both.
Not only did Eli clean his room, and he vacuumed the hall.
why_wrong: pairs "neither" with "or"
pairs "either" with "and"
completes "not only" with "and" instead of "but also"
explanation: "Whether ... or not" is a complete correlative pair. The others mismatch their pairs: "neither ... nor", "either ... or", "not only ... but also".

prompt: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: Ruby will call you as soon as she will get home.
After Owen had fed the fish, he washed his hands.
If Theo studied harder, he will pass the test.
Before the guests came, Mom cleans the whole kitchen.
why_wrong: puts "will" in a time clause about the future
mixes an unreal past condition with a "will" result
shifts to the present after a past time clause
explanation: "After Owen had fed the fish, he washed his hands" shows the order of two past actions correctly. The others need "as soon as she gets home", "If Theo studies harder, he will pass", and "Mom cleaned".

prompt: What part of speech is the bracketed word in the sentence?
passage: The bakery on the corner stays open [until] midnight on Fridays.
why_wrong: remembers that "until" can be a conjunction, but here it is followed by a noun, not a clause
thinks a time word must be an adverb
confuses a short word at a pause with an interjection
explanation: "Until" is followed by the noun "midnight", forming the prepositional phrase "until midnight", so it is a preposition. It would be a conjunction only before a clause ("until the baker leaves").

prompt: Which best describes the tense of the bracketed verb?
passage: By the end of the summer, Diego [will have read] twelve books from the library.
why_wrong: sees "will" and stops there, missing "have read"
sees "have" plus a past participle and misses "will"
confuses the perfect forms with each other
explanation: "Will have" plus the past participle "read" is the future perfect: an action completed before a future time (the end of the summer).

prompt: Which choice best combines the sentences without changing their meaning?
passage: The lemonade stand was busy all morning. Hana ran out of cups by noon.
choices: Although the lemonade stand was busy all morning, Hana ran out of cups by noon.
The lemonade stand was busy all morning until Hana ran out of cups by noon.
Because the lemonade stand was busy all morning, Hana ran out of cups by noon.
Hana ran out of cups by noon, so the lemonade stand was busy all morning.
why_wrong: joins the ideas with contrast, though running out of cups is what a busy stand would cause
adds a claim that the stand stopped being busy when the cups ran out
reverses cause and effect
explanation: A busy stand is the reason the cups ran out, so "because" keeps the meaning. "Although" signals a contrast, "until" adds a new claim, and the last choice makes running out the cause of the busy morning.
